lines.note: Hōrat na hito describes a person of unrestrained behavior, continuing the previous page's entry. The repeated &c. is printed here too; do not remove it merely because f211 also ends with &c.
Mal criado completes the description as ill-mannered or badly brought up. It does not mean that the person was physically made badly.
Hore, horuru, horeta first concerns loss of judgment or dotage. This historical inflection need not match the modern horeru paradigm; cadu continues caducar.
Oi ni horuru is becoming senile with age. Voini reflects the historical spelling of oi and is not an instruction to pronounce an additional modern v.
The first sense ends with old age; a second describes absorption in something. Item separates senses within the same verb, rather than introducing a fresh Japanese headword.

runs.text: transformado em algũa couſa que hum muito

lines.note: Transformado describes being carried away or absorbed by something loved. The scan's f and the Portuguese word support replacing OCR transſormado; the nasal mark in algũa is retained.

runs.text: ama, ou a que tem inclinação. Vt,

lines.note: The object may be loved or inclined toward. Hito ni begins the Japanese example of infatuation with a person, not a separate entry for hito.
Horuru completes hito ni horuru. The sense is having one's attention and affection wholly directed toward someone, connecting the mental and emotional senses of hore.
Ko ni horuru introduces excessive fondness for one's child. Coni is ko plus the particle ni, not a mysterious unsegmented noun.

runs.text: demaſiada affeição, & amor ao filho de ma-

lines.note: The Portuguese explicitly specifies excessive affection and love toward the child. Ma- continues maneira in the explanation of being beside oneself.

runs.text: neira que ande como fora deſi. ¶

lines.note: Neira completes maneira; fora deſi describes loss of composure. Foreta begins a new example, with its object and verb on the following row.
Horeta koto o yū is saying foolish things. Portuguese paruoices and deſba- support that reading; the final fragment continues deſbarates, not a new lexical item.
Rates completes deſbarates, foolish utterances. The short row closes the preceding example and is valid body text.
Horehoreto is an adverb describing being lost in love. Reduplication makes the connection to hore transparent without requiring a modernized transcription.

runs.text: de amores, ou com alguã outra affeição co-

lines.note: Other affections can also produce this state. The OCR's alguã is retained because the scan places the nasal mark toward the second vowel here; do not impose algũa mechanically.
On-kokoro mo haya begins a quoted example: the honored person's heart has already become absorbed. Alienado describes the emotional state, not a formal psychiatric diagnosis.
Horehoreto natte completes the quotation. The source label Taif. is upright and Lib. 18 is italic; the scan clearly has the numeral 8, not OCR B. The &c. is not Japanese to be kana-converted.
The translation describes the heart as transported or carried away. Trãsportado retains its printed nasal abbreviation and is not expanded in Level 1.
Horegoto is dispreferred in favor of horeta koto. Paruo- begins the Portuguese noun for foolishness; the preferred Japanese phrase remains roman.
Ice completes paruoice. The second synonym is deſbarate: enlargement shows the ascender and bowl of b where OCR supplied t.
Hōrei is an ordinary law or custom. The caron is retained from the scan; the final Fǒ- begins the example continued below.
Hōrei ni sugita koto means something exceeding the customary rule. The continuation joins the preceding Fǒ-; suguita is the expected voiced stem, not suquita.

runs.text: vai fora do cuſtume, ou modo ordinario.

lines.note: The Portuguese restates going outside custom or ordinary manner. This completes the comparative sense of sugita rather than adding a new meaning to koto.
Horemono is paraphrased horeta hito, someone whose judgment is impaired. The i marker introduces an explanatory equivalent, not part of the Japanese phrase.

runs.text: ou caduco, ou homem que por doença do àr, par

lines.note: The account mentions old age and historical illness attributed to air. Par continues parleſia on the next row; no absent hyphen is invented.

runs.text: leſia, &c. não eſta em ſeu perfeito juizo.

lines.note: Leſia completes the historical word for palsy. The definition says the person is not in full possession of judgment; its old medical account is reported, not endorsed.
An additional sense is a fool or simpleton. Item distinguishes that looser meaning from the preceding descriptions of illness and aging.
Hōren, teiō no teguruma, is the ruler's conveyance. The Japanese gloss and the following description identify a carried litter rather than a modern wheeled carriage alone.

runs.text: andas del Rey que leuão às coſtas, ou aos

lines.note: The royal litter is borne on people's backs or shoulders. The printed accent on às is retained rather than silently modernizing the surrounding orthography.
Ombros completes the description, shoulders. This very short continuation still belongs to the litter definition.

runs.text: O caducar dos velhos, ou leſão do

lines.note: Horeke is the dotage of old people or an impairment of judgment. Its final qe represents ke, distinct from the qe-less verb hore above.
The impairment is again attributed to historical doença de ar. Horeke ga begins an example with the subject particle ga.
Horeke ga saita, or tsuita, describes the onset of dotage. The alternative forms are printed examples, not an invitation to replace saita with a modern expression.

runs.text: deſtampado o velho, ou leſo no juizo por al-

lines.note: The translation describes an old person losing sound judgment or someone impaired through illness. The final al continues algũa below.
The illness examples include parleſia. The scan has an i after ſ, not OCR t in parleſta; dear remains the visibly joined de ar.
Hōri, nori no kotowari, means the principles or reasons of a law. The Japanese gloss explains the compound without requiring a change to printed Razoens daley.
Hori is a ditch; hori o horu means digging it. Caua is the Portuguese gloss even though it is set upright here, so its appearance must not be mistaken for Japanese kawa.
Hori o umuru means filling the ditch. The older verb form umuru is supported by the Portuguese entulhar and should not be modernized to umeru.
Hori, horu, hotta concerns carving or engraving. The abbreviated endings list the inflection, with ru supplied through the entry's r plus the printed u.
The next hori is digging or mining. Its explicitly printed ru differs from the preceding entry's u; preserve that distinction rather than regularizing the paradigms.
Horiage means making relief work. The generated kana may over-join ri+a; morphologically this is hori plus age, as the carving sense indicates.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Acabar de cauar, ou de fazer

lines.note: A second sense is finishing excavation. Ag(e) can express completion here, not simply upward motion.

runs.text: algũa caua, ou outra obra a enxada: ou aca-

lines.note: The excavation may be a ditch or other hoe-work. The scan has a colon after enxada, corrected from the OCR period; aca- begins acabar.

runs.text: bar deabrir, ou fazer obra de releuo.

lines.note: Bar completes acabar; finishing engraving or relief work is also included. Deabrir is retained as printed, rather than respaced merely for modern readability.
Horiake, horiakeru, means opening or clearing by digging. The scan has Foriaqe, with i rather than OCR t in Fortaqe; the kana failure helped expose the malformed reading.
Baracar completes esbaracar, a historical form in the sense of clearing away. No cedilla is added solely from modern desembaraçar.
Horikaeshi turns soil over by digging. The printed eita past ending is retained; ter- continues terra across the column boundary.
Ta o horikaesu is turning the soil of a field. Ra completes the preceding column's terra; the Japanese example is continuous across that column boundary.

runs.text: varzeas virar a terra de baixo pera cima.

lines.note: The soil is turned from underneath to the top in wet fields. Varzeas gives the agricultural setting rather than a new Japanese noun.
Horikuzushi means breaking down by digging. The printed uita past ending is a historical inflection, not an OCR error to modernize to ushita.
A mountain or ridge can be cut away. Serra here is topographical alongside monte, rather than the saw tool sense of the same Portuguese word.
Horig(i)wa is the edge of a ditch. Gui represents gi before the following glide spelling ua; the Portuguese borda is a straightforward confirmation.
Horiidashi means digging something out. The written ij spans the compound's vowel sequence; the entry is not horijidashi with an inserted consonant.
Dōtetsu o horiidasu is extracting copper and iron. Final t in Dôtetuo participates in the Japanese compound before the object marker, not a missing modern su that should be supplied.
The metals are taken from a mine. Per begins the Latin register phrase per met., announcing a metaphorical extension on the next row.

runs.text: met. Achar, ou deſcobrir algũa couſa noua,

lines.note: Met. completes per met.: finding or discovering something new metaphorically. The verb retains a sense of uncovering, even when no literal digging occurs.
A tea-ceremony object is the example of such a discovery. Chanoyu is visibly italic within the Portuguese explanation; do not automatically romanize it from earlier pages.
Horiire means putting something into a dug place. The two i vowels belong to the joining of hori and ire, not a geminated consonant.
Enterrar supplies the concise equivalent, burying. This short row completes the definition rather than being an isolated entry.
Horimawashi is digging around. The scan reads roda, a circle or circuit, rather than OCR rada; the Japanese mawashi provides independent contextual support.
Horimekashi causes a crunching sound in the teeth. This is a causative sound verb, not another excavation compound despite its alphabetic position.

runs.text: tes, ou ſoar algũa couſa como obreas, ou paſ-

lines.note: Wafers and small birds exemplify things that crunch. Tes completes dentes; paſ- continues the bird word below.

runs.text: ſarinhos que ſe comem com os oßos, &c.

lines.note: The small birds are eaten with their bones. Oßos contains the joined double-s shape already represented by ß; retain it rather than expanding by habit.

Horimeki is the corresponding intransitive crunching. The enlarged row shows a damaged final m but no separate trailing hyphen; the complete Portuguese Trincarem belongs in italic, including its capital T.
Similar things make the sound in one's teeth. Nos dentes confirms that the preceding ſoarem is complete, not a word awaiting a suffix here.
Horimono is sculpture or relief work. The final Fo- begins the Japanese example and should not be read as part of the Portuguese gloss.
Horimono o suru is doing carving. The continuation rimonouo joins the preceding Fo-, and the object particle is part of the Japanese example.
De releuo completes making relief work. Its short physical row remains body text, with neither letters nor an inferred headword added.
Hōrin o tenzuru is turning the Dharma wheel, expressed here as spreading the doctrine. Tenzuru is intelligible Japanese; the circumflex spelling is preserved.

runs.text: diuulgar a ley, ou doutrina do Fotoque.

lines.note: The law or teaching belongs to the Fotoque. The word is italic in this scan even though other pages use roman type for the same Japanese borrowing.
Horinoke removes or sets aside by digging. Portuguese afastar matches the transitive noke component, not a different headword with g.
Hōryō is quantity or limit. Qiri starts the expression continued below; the Japanese conceptual pairing is extent and boundary, not a personal name.

runs.text: Não tem fim nem limite, ou

lines.note: Kiri, hōryō ga nai describes having no end or limit. The damaged initial has an ascender consistent with f rather than OCR r; retain the uncertain unmarked first o rather than supplying an accent solely from the headword.
He infinito restates the lack of a limit. This is the final gloss of the preceding Japanese expression, not a mathematical definition added by the reviewer.
Hōriki, nori no chikara, is the power or efficacy of the law. The q in riqi corresponds to ki; there is no reason to change it to g.
Da ley completes the doctrinal power gloss. The row's brevity does not make it page furniture.
Horikiri cuts or blocks a route by digging. The Japanese inflection and the Portuguese description both indicate a transitive action.
Do completes tomando: taking up or obstructing the path. The object caminho confirms the military or defensive excavation sense.

runs.text: Caua, ou maneira de coua aberta que

lines.note: The noun horikiri is an open trench or ditch. It is distinct from the preceding verb even though the romanized forms match.

runs.text: eſtà nos caminhos pera não paßar gẽte, ou bestas.

lines.note: The trench stops people or animals from passing along roads. Beſtas would not mean foolish people in this context; retain the printed bestas and the OCR's ß in paßar.
Horisukashi is openwork carving. Eſculpir is visible in the scan where OCR read Eſoulpir; the Japanese sukashi and the following through-opening explanation agree.

runs.text: maneira que paſſe de parte a parte.

lines.note: The carving passes from side to side. The double-s is a single joined beta-like shape, so paße distinguishes it from separately printed ſſ under the project's convention.
Horisute throws something away by digging it out. The historical tçuru ending is preserved rather than replaced with modern teru.
Horitaoshi undermines or digs something down. The stem tauoxi is the expected historical taoshi form, not a typo induced by modern spelling.
Trees and houses are examples of things brought down. Derrubar gives the physical effect of undermining them.
Horitsuke is engraving or carving into a surface. The following buril specifies an engraving tool, supporting this sense of tsuke.
The burin closes the first sense. Horitsukuru and the following hori- compound introduce reaching a place by excavation; the printed alternative marker is kept.
Horito(d)okuru completes the alternative, reaching a specified point by digging. Tè is the printed Portuguese shortened form of até and should not be expanded.
Horitōshi passes through by tunneling or boring. Ou continues outra below and does not require an invented final hyphen.

runs.text: tra banda, ou abrindo com ferro furar.

lines.note: Tra completes outra banda, the other side. Ferro denotes the tool used to pierce through, not a separate material gloss for the Japanese headword.
Hōryū, nori no nagare, is a branch or lineage of a doctrine. Enlargement shows the damaged i before ù; OCR Fôrſù inserted a long s and lost the intelligible ryū sequence. NINJAL corroborates Fôriù.
The branch belongs to a particular sect. Particular has a faint but recoverable u where OCR omitted it; the worn printing should not create particalar.
Hori-umaya is a farmer's excavated stable. The initial v of vmaya is vocalic; the definition describes its construction, not a different word umaya.

runs.text: por baixo, ou ſem taboado, & c.

lines.note: The stable is dug below ground or lacks a boarded floor. The scan supports baixo and tabuado, correcting OCR bamco and tabaado; the separate Fori- underneath is a catchword, not this line's continuation.
